A few days ago, an engineer I work with sent me a message that read almost like an apology.

He does excellent work with AI, often well outside his role, and the people around him are ambitious, so of course they want some of it. Several times a week, someone asks him which skills and workflows he uses. And he has nothing to send them. His whole setup is him, the model and a lot of hours. People don't quite believe him, and every time he says it, he feels like he's turning them away.

I'll be honest: at first I didn't believe him either.

So I asked how he got to some design files I really liked. He started with a prompt as vague as his thoughts, got back something unusable, then spent long hours (and about half a billion tokens) refining what he wanted, where, why and how. Over and over.

So that's all you.

My next thought was: fine, then let's write it down. Let AI read his conversations, learn how he iterates, and get to his level faster next time.

He pushed back, and he had a point tbh. People seem sure a developer's job fits in a skill file, yet nobody tries to write their own job down as a thousand-line markdown file. I certainly can't write a skill that runs product (some days I'd love to).

Where we landed reminded me of something every Italian family has: a nonna whose ragù nobody can reproduce. She'll happily give you the recipe. You can read it, tweak it, borrow ideas from it. Hers, though, was tuned over decades to her pot, her butcher and her taste, and none of that comes with the recipe.

A skill file is the recipe. A lot of how you work does fit in it. What's hard to write down is how you react to a new situation , because that depends on the situation, and the model has already read all the same cookbooks you have.

## The Sundays

I learned this building Triagon, an agent that triages our front desk requests, the questions colleagues bring to product every day. The goal was simple: answer fast and accurately. The first results were noisy. It missed context, replied when it shouldn't, and didn't sound like me at all.

Getting it right took a lot of work: teaching it to reply only when needed, to gather the context it needs before answering, and to answer in my voice.

Each fix was small. Each one made the next answer a bit better, and none of them went away. Every correction stays , so every week starts a little higher than the one before. That's the part that compounds, and it's the part nobody can copy from someone else's file.

I do the same with my own work now. I keep adding to a context of how I work and why I decide things the way I do, one correction at a time.

## Other people's recipes

There are now plenty of places to download other people's skills. I think they're useful. They show you what's possible, and a good one can save you a week.

The risk is that you skip the cooking. Personalising your setup is a muscle , and you only train it by iterating on your own problems. A downloaded skill feeds you today. Building your own keeps feeding you.

## Patience

The annoying thing about compounding is that early on it looks like nothing. The first weeks are mostly labor, and the output is often worse than if you'd done the work yourself. That's where most people stop, and go ask someone else for their skill file.

Nobody's first ragù tastes like nonna's. Yours gets good somewhere around the twentieth Sunday.

He still doesn't have a skill to share, and neither do I. What we have is a lot of Sundays. The returns come later than you'd like, and they're bigger than you'd expect.
